exercises.prompt: Words are sorted in an unknown alphabet. Return the letters (all letters that appear) in an order consistent with it; if several orders work, return the alphabetically smallest; return "" if the input is invalid.
hints: Compare each pair of neighbouring words: the first differing letters give one ordering rule (an edge).
Topologically sort the letters; a cycle (or a longer word before its own prefix) means invalid.
Approach: Build edges from adjacent words, then topological sort (heap for the smallest order).

exercises.title: BFS on weighted edges
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test ag-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
BFS fixes a distance the first time it reaches a node, which is the fewest EDGES, not the smallest total weight
A → B (10) is found before A → C → B (1 + 1). Use Dijkstra.

exercises.title: Union without find
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test ag-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
parent[b] = a re-links b itself instead of joining the two ROOTS, which can cut b away from its old group
With pairs (0, 1) then (2, 1), node 1 leaves 0’s group. Union the roots: parent[find(b)] = find(a).

exercises.title: A cycle goes unnoticed
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test ag-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
With a cycle some courses never reach in-degree 0, and it silently returns a partial order instead of reporting failure
Check len(order) == n; otherwise return [] (impossible).

exercises.title: Activity Selection
exercises.prompt: Each activity is `[start, end]`. Two activities are compatible if one starts at or after the other ends. Return the largest number of compatible activities.
hints: Which activity should you do first to leave the most room for the rest?
Sort by end time; keep an activity if it starts at or after the last kept end.
Approach: Sort by end time and greedily take every compatible activity.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the sorted copy
mistakes: Sorting by start time or by length.
Using start > last_end, which rejects back-to-back activities.
exercises.followup: Return the chosen activities themselves, not just how many.

exercises.title: Make Change (canonical coins)
exercises.prompt: The coin system is canonical (like 1, 5, 10, 25), so taking the largest coin that fits is optimal. Return the coins used, largest first. The coins may be given in any order and always include 1.
hints: Sort the coins from largest to smallest first.
Take each coin as many times as it fits.
Approach: Largest coin first, as many times as it fits. Only correct because the coin system is canonical.
exercises.cx: O(k log k + number of coins used) time
mistakes: Forgetting to sort coins that arrive in a random order.
Believing this works for any coins: [1, 3, 4] with amount 6 breaks it.
exercises.followup: Write a brute force that finds the true minimum for small amounts and use it to find the smallest amount where greedy fails for coins [1, 3, 4].

exercises.title: Lemonade Change
exercises.prompt: Lemonade costs $5. Customers pay with $5, $10 or $20 bills, in order, and you start with no change. Return `True` if you can give everyone correct change.
hints: You only need to count $5 and $10 bills ($20 bills are never given as change).
For $20, which change should you give first: $10 + $5, or three $5s?
Approach: Count bills; for $20 give $10 + $5 when possible because $5 bills are more useful later.
mistakes: Spending three $5 bills when a $10 + $5 is available.
Counting $20 bills as change.
exercises.followup: What if lemonade costs $10 and customers can pay with $10, $20 or $50?

exercises.title: Maximum Units on a Truck
exercises.prompt: `box_types[i] = [count, units_per_box]`. The truck holds at most `truck_size` boxes. Return the most units you can load.
hints: Every box takes one slot, so prefer boxes with more units.
Sort by units per box, descending, and fill up.
Approach: Greedy by units per box: since all boxes have the same size, the best boxes first is optimal.
mistakes: Sorting by count instead of units per box.
Not stopping when the truck is full (taking negative amounts).
exercises.followup: Why does the same greedy fail if boxes have different sizes?

exercises.title: Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons
exercises.prompt: Each balloon covers `[start, end]` on the x-axis. An arrow shot at x bursts every balloon with start ≤ x ≤ end. Return the fewest arrows that burst all balloons.
hints: Shoot the first arrow at the end of the balloon that ends first.
Sort by end. A balloon needs a new arrow only if it starts after the last arrow’s position.
Approach: Like activity selection: sort by end, place an arrow at each group’s first end.
mistakes: Using >= instead of >: touching balloons share an arrow.
Sorting by start without tracking the minimum end.
exercises.followup: How is this related to "minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap"?

exercises.title: Boats to Save People
exercises.prompt: Each boat carries at most two people with total weight ≤ `limit`. Every person weighs at most `limit`. Return the fewest boats.
hints: The heaviest person must go in some boat. Who is the best partner for them?
Sort, then pair the lightest with the heaviest when they fit.
Approach: Sort and use two pointers: the heaviest person leaves every round, taking the lightest along if possible.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space for the sorted copy
mistakes: while i < j, which forgets the last single person.
Trying to pair the two heaviest people.
exercises.followup: What changes if a boat can carry any number of people up to the weight limit? (Hint: it becomes bin packing, which is NP-hard.)

exercises.title: Minimum Train Platforms
exercises.prompt: Train k arrives at `arr[k]` and departs at `dep[k]`, occupying a platform for the whole closed interval. A train arriving at the same time another departs needs a different platform. Return the fewest platforms needed.
hints: Only the order of events matters: arrivals and departures.
Sort both lists and sweep through time, counting trains present.
Approach: Sweep line over sorted arrivals and departures, tracking the number of trains present.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
mistakes: Using < instead of <= and sharing a platform at the exact same minute.
Sorting the (arr, dep) pairs together and comparing neighbours only.
exercises.followup: Solve it with a min-heap of departure times (see Meeting Rooms II, hp-meeting-rooms).

exercises.title: Fractional Knapsack
exercises.prompt: Items are `(value, weight)`. You may take any fraction of an item. Return the largest total value that fits in `capacity`, as a float.
hints: Which item gives the most value per unit of weight?
Take best-ratio items whole while they fit, then a fraction of the next one.
Approach: Sort by value / weight descending and fill the bag greedily.
mistakes: Sorting by value or by weight instead of by ratio.
Using integer division and losing the fractional part.
exercises.followup: Show with a small example why this greedy is wrong for 0/1 knapsack, then solve 0/1 knapsack with DP (topic 20).

exercises.title: Largest Number
exercises.prompt: Arrange the non-negative integers so that, concatenated, they form the largest number. Return it as a string without leading zeros.
hints: Sorting numerically or as plain strings both fail (try 3 and 30).
Put a before b when str(a) + str(b) > str(b) + str(a).
Approach: Sort the strings with a comparator on a + b versus b + a, then join; handle all zeros.
exercises.cx: O(n log n · L) time where L is the number of digits
mistakes: Returning "00" for [0, 0].
Sorting strings in reverse order: "30" would come before "3".
exercises.followup: Prove the comparator is transitive (so sorting with it is valid).

exercises.title: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
exercises.prompt: Each job `(deadline, profit)` takes one unit of time and must finish by its deadline (time slots are 1, 2, 3, …). Do at most one job per slot. Return the largest total profit.
hints: Consider the most profitable jobs first.
Put each job in the latest free slot not after its deadline, leaving earlier slots for jobs with tight deadlines.
Approach: Sort by profit descending; place each job in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline.
exercises.cx: O(n²) time in the worst case, O(n) space
mistakes: Putting a job in the earliest free slot, which blocks urgent jobs.
Sorting by deadline instead of profit.
exercises.followup: Speed up "latest free slot" with a union-find over slots to get about O(n log n).

exercises.title: Two City Scheduling
exercises.prompt: `costs[i] = [a, b]` is the cost of flying person i to city A or city B. Exactly half the people (the list length is even) must go to each city. Return the minimum total cost.
hints: Imagine everyone goes to B first. Sending person i to A instead changes the cost by a − b.
Send the n people with the smallest a − b to A.
Approach: Sort by a − b and send the first half to A, the rest to B.
mistakes: Sending each person to their cheaper city, which ignores the half-and-half rule.
Sorting by a alone.
exercises.followup: What if city A takes exactly k people instead of half?

exercises.title: Candy
exercises.prompt: Children stand in a line with ratings. Each child gets at least one candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more candies than that neighbour. Return the fewest candies needed.
hints: Handle one neighbour at a time: first everyone versus their left neighbour.
Then a right-to-left pass for the right neighbour, taking the max so the first rule still holds.
Approach: Two greedy passes: left-to-right for left neighbours, right-to-left for right neighbours, keeping the maximum.
mistakes: A single pass, which cannot see a later lower neighbour.
Overwriting the left-pass value instead of taking the max.
Giving more candy for an equal rating (not required).
exercises.followup: Solve it in O(1) extra space by counting the lengths of rising and falling runs.
exercises.dry:
ratings     1  3  4  5  2
left pass   1  2  3  4  1
right pass  1  2  3  4  1   (only index 3 checks 5 > 2: max(4, 2) = 4)
sum = 11

exercises.title: Sorted by the wrong end
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test gr-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It sorts by start time; one long early interval blocks everything. Sort by end time.
With [[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]] it picks [1, 10] and stops at 1. Sorting by end picks [2, 3] and [4, 5].

exercises.title: The last passenger is left behind
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test gr-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
When i == j one person is still waiting, but the loop has stopped: use while i <= j
With weights [1, 2, 2, 3] and limit 3 the pointers meet on one person who never gets a boat.

exercises.title: Spending the wrong change
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test gr-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
For $20 it spends three $5 bills before trying $10 + $5. Fives are more useful (they are needed for $10 bills), so give $10 + $5 first.
Greedy choice: keep the most flexible coin. With [5, 5, 5, 5, 10, 20, 10] the buggy version has no $5 left for the last customer.

exercises.title: Fibonacci with Memoization
exercises.prompt: Return the n-th Fibonacci number (`fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`). Plain recursion is far too slow for n = 90: cache your results.
hints: Write the plain recursive version first.
Add @lru_cache(maxsize=None) from functools, or store results in a dict.
Approach: Memoized recursion: each fib(k) is computed once.
mistakes: Leaving out the cache: fib(90) would take longer than the age of the universe.
Wrong base cases, e.g. fib(0) = 1.
exercises.followup: Write it bottom-up with two variables: O(n) time and O(1) space.

exercises.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
exercises.prompt: `cost[i]` is the price of stepping on stair i. You may start on stair 0 or 1, and from each stair climb 1 or 2 steps. Return the minimum cost to reach the top (just past the last stair).
hints: Define dp[i] as the cheapest total to stand on stair i.
dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2]). The top is one step past the end.
Approach: 1D DP over stairs; the answer is the cheaper of the last two stairs.
exercises.cx: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(1) with two variables)
mistakes: Returning dp[-1] only: you may also jump to the top from the second-to-last stair.
Adding the cost of the top, which is free.
exercises.followup: Reduce the space to O(1).

exercises.title: House Robber
exercises.prompt: Houses in a row hold `nums[i]` money. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the most money you can take.
hints: At each house you either rob it (and add the best total from two houses back) or skip it.
best(i) = max(best(i − 1), best(i − 2) + nums[i]).
Approach: 1D DP; only the previous two values are needed, so use two variables.
mistakes: Taking every other house (even or odd positions): [2, 1, 1, 2] needs houses 0 and 3.
Mishandling an empty list or a single house.
exercises.followup: House Robber II: the houses are in a circle (dp-robber-circle).

exercises.title: House Robber II (circle)
exercises.prompt: Same as House Robber, but the houses form a circle: the first and last houses are neighbours.
hints: You can never rob both the first and the last house.
Solve two straight-line problems: without the first house, and without the last.
Approach: Reduce the circle to two line problems and take the better one.
exercises.cx: O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the slices
mistakes: Forgetting the single-house case (both slices are empty).
Subtracting something instead of splitting into two cases.
exercises.followup: What if the houses form a binary tree and you cannot rob a parent and child together?

exercises.title: Decode Ways
exercises.prompt: A message of letters is encoded as numbers: A = 1, …, Z = 26. Given a string of digits, return how many ways it can be decoded. "06" is not a valid code for F.
hints: The last letter used either one digit or two digits.
ways(i) = ways(i − 1) if s[i] is 1–9, plus ways(i − 2) if the last two digits form 10–26.
Approach: 1D DP like climbing stairs, with validity checks for one-digit and two-digit steps.
mistakes: Treating "0" as a letter on its own.
Allowing two-digit codes like "05" or "27".
exercises.followup: Return one valid decoding as letters, or all of them for short strings.

exercises.title: Coin Change (fewest coins)
exercises.prompt: Return the fewest coins that add up to `amount`, using any number of each coin. Return −1 if it is impossible.
hints: Greedy fails for coins like [1, 3, 4]. Think about the last coin used.
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a − c]) over coins c ≤ a; dp[0] = 0, everything else starts at infinity.
Approach: Unbounded DP over amounts 0..amount.
mistakes: Starting dp at 0 instead of infinity.
Returning infinity instead of −1.
Using greedy.
exercises.followup: Also return which coins to use (store the last coin chosen for each amount).

exercises.title: Coin Change II (number of ways)
exercises.prompt: Return the number of combinations of coins that make `amount` (order does not matter: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are the same).
hints: dp[a] = number of ways to make a. dp[0] = 1.
Loop over coins on the outside, amounts on the inside; with the loops swapped you count orderings instead.
Approach: Unbounded knapsack counting: add dp[a − c] for each coin c, with coins in the outer loop.
mistakes: Swapping the loops, which counts 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 separately.
dp[0] = 0, which makes every answer 0.
exercises.followup: Count ordered sequences instead (that is "Combination Sum IV"). Which loop order do you need?

exercises.title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
exercises.prompt: Move only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Cells with 1 are blocked. Return the number of paths.
hints: paths(r, c) = paths(r − 1, c) + paths(r, c − 1), and 0 on a blocked cell.
You only need one row of the table if you update it left to right.
Approach: Grid DP with a single rolling row.
mistakes: Setting the whole first row/column to 1 even after an obstacle.
Forgetting that the start or the end itself may be blocked.
exercises.followup: Return the path count modulo 10⁹ + 7 for a 1000 × 1000 grid.

exercises.title: Minimum Path Sum
exercises.prompt: Move only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right. Return the smallest possible sum of the numbers on your path.
hints: A cell is entered from above or from the left.
dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r − 1][c], dp[r][c − 1]); the first row and column have only one option.
Approach: Grid DP taking the cheaper of the two incoming neighbours.
mistakes: Greedily stepping to the smaller neighbour, which can lead into an expensive region.
Treating the first row/column like inner cells (index −1 wraps around in Python!).
exercises.followup: Print the path itself by walking back from the bottom-right cell.

exercises.title: Longest Common Subsequence
exercises.prompt: Return the length of the longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order (not necessarily next to each other).
hints: Compare the last characters of the two prefixes.
If they match: 1 + LCS of both prefixes shortened. Otherwise: the better of dropping one character from either string.
Approach: 2D DP over prefixes with an extra row and column for empty prefixes.
mistakes: Comparing a[i] with b[j] instead of a[i − 1] with b[j − 1].
Confusing subsequence with substring (contiguous).
exercises.followup: Reconstruct one LCS string by walking back through the table.

exercises.title: 0/1 Knapsack
exercises.prompt: Each item has a value and a weight and can be taken at most once. Return the largest total value with total weight ≤ `capacity`.
hints: For each item: skip it, or take it and add its value to the best answer for capacity − weight.
A 2D table dp[i][c] works. A 1D table works too if capacity goes downwards.
Approach: Classic 0/1 knapsack DP over capacities.
mistakes: Looping capacity upwards with a 1D table (items get reused).
Using greedy by value/weight ratio, which is wrong for 0/1.
exercises.followup: Return which items to take. (Keep the 2D table, then walk back.)
exercises.dry:
values [1, 4, 5, 7], weights [1, 3, 4, 5], capacity 7
best: weights 3 + 4 = 7, values 4 + 5 = 9

exercises.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
exercises.prompt: Return `True` if the list can be split into two groups with equal sums.
hints: If the total is odd, the answer is no. Otherwise: is there a subset summing to total / 2?
That is a 0/1 knapsack with booleans: reachable sums.
Approach: Subset-sum DP over sums 0..total/2, iterating sums downwards.
mistakes: Forgetting the odd-total shortcut.
Iterating sums upwards, which lets one number be used twice.
exercises.followup: Use a Python int as a bitset: reach |= reach << x. Why does that work?

exercises.title: Target Sum
exercises.prompt: Put a + or − in front of every number. Return how many ways the expression can equal `target`.
hints: Brute force tries 2ⁿ sign choices. Many lead to the same running sum.
Keep a dict: running sum → number of ways, and update it for each number.
Approach: DP over the set of reachable running sums (counting).
exercises.cx: O(n · S) time and space where S = sum(nums)
mistakes: Forgetting that 0 can take both signs (two ways).
Using a list indexed by sum without an offset for negative sums.
exercises.followup: Turn it into subset sum: the positive part P satisfies P = (sum + target) / 2.

exercises.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
exercises.prompt: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: Let best[i] be the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i.
best[i] = 1 + max(best[j]) over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
Approach: O(n²) DP over end positions; the answer is the max over all ends.
mistakes: Returning best[-1]: the longest subsequence may end anywhere.
Using <= and counting equal values (the sequence must be strictly increasing).
exercises.followup: Solve it in O(n log n) (dp-lis-fast).

exercises.title: Largest Square of Ones
exercises.prompt: Return the area of the largest square containing only 1s in a grid of 0s and 1s.
hints: Let side[r][c] be the side of the largest all-ones square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c).
It is 1 + the minimum of the squares ending above, to the left and diagonally above-left.
Approach: 2D DP on bottom-right corners; return the best side squared.
mistakes: Returning the side instead of the area.
Taking the max of the three neighbours instead of the min.
exercises.followup: Count all squares of ones (of every size) in the grid.

exercises.title: Word Break
exercises.prompt: Return `True` if `s` can be split into a sequence of words from `words` (words may be reused).
hints: ok[i] means the first i characters can be split into words.
ok[i] is True if some j < i has ok[j] True and s[j:i] is a word.
Approach: 1D DP over prefix lengths with a set for O(1) word lookups.
exercises.cx: O(n · L) slice checks where L is the longest word length
mistakes: A greedy "take the longest word first" (fails on "cars" with ca, rs, car).
Plain recursion without memoization: exponential on "aaaa…b".
exercises.followup: Return all possible sentences (memoize lists of splits per start index).

exercises.title: Maximum Product Subarray
exercises.prompt: Return the largest product of a non-empty contiguous subarray.
hints: Like Kadane, but a negative number turns the smallest product into the largest.
Track both the max and the min product of a subarray ending at each index.
Approach: DP with two states per index: max and min product ending here.
mistakes: Tracking only the maximum (fails on [-2, 3, -4]).
Updating hi before computing lo with the old hi.
exercises.followup: Return the subarray itself, not just its product.

exercises.title: Edit Distance
exercises.prompt: Return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and replacements needed to turn `a` into `b`.
hints: Base cases: turning a prefix into an empty string costs its length.
If the last characters match, no cost; otherwise 1 + the best of delete, insert and replace.
Approach: 2D DP over prefixes (Levenshtein distance).
mistakes: Forgetting the base row and column.
Adding 1 even when the characters match.
exercises.followup: Use only two rows of the table: O(m) space.

exercises.title: LIS in O(n log n)
exercises.prompt: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, for lists of up to 100,000 numbers.
hints: Keep, for each length, the smallest possible last element of an increasing run of that length.
That list is sorted, so find where x goes with bisect_left.
Approach: Patience sorting: maintain the sorted tails list with binary search.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
mistakes: bisect_right, which allows equal values (non-strict increase).
Thinking tails is itself an increasing subsequence of the input (it is not).
exercises.followup: Recover an actual longest subsequence, not only its length.

exercises.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
exercises.prompt: Return the length of the longest subsequence of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards.
hints: Interval DP: the state is a substring s[i..j].
If the ends match, they wrap the best answer for the inside; otherwise drop one end.
Approach: Interval DP filled from short substrings to long ones (or: LCS of s and reversed s).
mistakes: Filling i from 0 upwards, which reads dp[i + 1][…] before it is computed.
Confusing it with the longest palindromic substring (contiguous).
exercises.followup: Show that the answer equals lcs(s, s[::-1]), and find the minimum insertions to make s a palindrome.

exercises.title: Zero coins for everything
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test dp-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
dp starts at 0 for every amount, so min() never improves on 0: start at infinity (except dp[0] = 0)
For a minimisation, unknown states must start at +infinity. Only the base case dp[0] = 0 is truly zero.

exercises.title: A robber with the wrong start
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test dp-d4` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
dp[1] must be the best of the first two houses, max(nums[0], nums[1]), not nums[1]
dp[i] means "best total using houses 0..i". With only two houses you take the richer one.

exercises.title: LCS shifted by one
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test dp-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
Row i stands for the prefix a[:i], whose last character is a[i − 1], not a[i]
The table has an extra row and column for empty prefixes, so string indexes are shifted by one: compare a[i − 1] with b[j − 1].

exercises.title: The item that was packed three times
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test dp-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
The capacity loop goes upwards, so dp[cap − w] may already include this item: each item can be reused. Loop downwards.
With values [10], weights [1] and capacity 3 the buggy version returns 30. Looping from capacity down to w keeps every item 0/1.

exercises.title: Number of 1 Bits
exercises.prompt: Return how many 1 bits a non-negative integer has, without `bin()` or `bit_count()`.
hints: Check the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift right.
Faster: n & (n − 1) removes one set bit per step.
Approach: Kernighan's trick: clear the lowest set bit until n is 0.
exercises.cx: O(k) time where k is the number of set bits, O(1) space
mistakes: Using n / 2 (float) instead of n >> 1 or n // 2.
Looping a fixed 32 times and missing higher bits of a 64-bit value.
exercises.followup: Count the 1 bits of every number from 0 to n in O(n) (bit-counting-bits).

exercises.title: Power of Two
exercises.prompt: Return `True` if n is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …), using a bitwise test instead of a loop.
hints: A power of two has exactly one 1 bit.
n & (n − 1) clears that bit; zero and negatives are not powers of two.
Approach: n > 0 and (n & (n − 1)) == 0.
mistakes: Forgetting n > 0 (0 & −1 == 0).
Using n % 2 == 0, which is also true for 6.
exercises.followup: Is n a power of four? (One set bit, at an even position: n & 0x55555555.)

exercises.title: Single Number
exercises.prompt: Every value appears exactly twice except one, which appears once. Return it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: What is x ^ x? What is x ^ 0?
XOR all the numbers together.
Approach: XOR everything: duplicates cancel out.
mistakes: Using a set or Counter: correct, but O(n) space.
Starting result at 1 instead of 0.
exercises.followup: Every value appears three times except one (bit-single-ii).

exercises.title: Missing Number
exercises.prompt: The list contains n distinct numbers from 0..n, so exactly one is missing. Return it using XOR (or a sum), in O(1) extra space.
hints: XOR all numbers 0..n with all the list elements.
Everything appears twice except the missing number.
Approach: XOR of the full range with the list; or n(n + 1)/2 − sum(nums).
mistakes: Forgetting to include n in the range.
Sorting first (O(n log n)).
exercises.followup: Two numbers are missing. Find both with XOR (see bit-two-singles).

exercises.title: Get, Set, Clear, Toggle
exercises.prompt: Write four one-line functions for bit i (0 = lowest): `get_bit(n, i)` returns 0 or 1; `set_bit`, `clear_bit` and `toggle_bit` return the new number.
hints: Every operation uses the mask 1 << i.
get: shift and AND 1. set: OR. clear: AND with the inverted mask. toggle: XOR.
Approach: Build the mask 1 << i and combine it with &, |, ^ or ~.
mistakes: clear_bit with n & (1 << i), which keeps only that bit.
Returning n & (1 << i) from get_bit (that is 2ⁱ, not 1).
exercises.followup: Clear all bits above i, or all bits from i down to 0, with one mask each.

exercises.title: Hamming Distance
exercises.prompt: Return the number of bit positions where x and y differ.
hints: XOR marks the positions where two bits differ.
Count the 1 bits of x ^ y.
Approach: Popcount of x ^ y.
mistakes: Comparing decimal digits instead of bits.
exercises.followup: Sum of Hamming distances over all pairs in a list, in O(32 · n): count ones and zeros per bit position.

exercises.title: Counting Bits 0..n
exercises.prompt: Return a list where element i is the number of 1 bits in i, for every i from 0 to n, in O(n) total.
hints: i >> 1 is i with its lowest bit removed, and it is smaller than i.
bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1): a DP that reuses earlier answers.
Approach: DP on numbers: reuse the answer for i >> 1.
mistakes: Recounting every number from scratch: O(n log n).
Writing bits[i // 2] + i % 2 is fine, but i / 2 is a float index.
exercises.followup: Use bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1 instead. Why does it work?

exercises.title: Reverse 32 Bits
exercises.prompt: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer (bit 0 becomes bit 31, and so on) and return the result.
hints: Take bits from the right end of n one at a time.
Append each to result by shifting result left first. Do it exactly 32 times, even if n becomes 0.
Approach: 32 iterations of: shift result left, add the lowest bit of n, shift n right.
mistakes: Stopping when n becomes 0 (leading zeros matter).
Using bin(n)[::-1] without padding to 32 bits.
exercises.followup: If this is called millions of times, cache the reversal of each byte (256 entries).

exercises.title: Gray Code
exercises.prompt: Return the n-bit Gray code sequence starting at 0: all 2ⁿ numbers, where consecutive numbers differ in exactly one bit. Use the standard reflected Gray code.
hints: There is a direct formula for the i-th Gray code.
Approach: Formula i ^ (i >> 1) for i in 0 .. 2ⁿ − 1.
exercises.cx: O(2ⁿ) time and space (the output size)
mistakes: Generating by trial and error, which may not match the standard order.
exercises.followup: Build the sequence by reflection: Gray(n) = Gray(n − 1) followed by its reverse with the top bit set.

tests.call: all(bin(a ^ b).count("1") == 1 for a, b in zip(gray_code(10), gray_code(10)[1:]))

exercises.title: Add Without +
exercises.prompt: Return a + b for non-negative integers without using `+`, `-` or `sum()`: use XOR for the sum without carries and AND + shift for the carries.
hints: XOR adds bits without carrying; AND finds where a carry happens.
Repeat with (a ^ b, (a & b) << 1) until there is no carry.
Approach: Ripple-carry addition with XOR and AND.
mistakes: Forgetting to shift the carry left.
Running it on negative numbers in Python: unbounded ints never stop carrying (mask to 32 bits if you need negatives).
exercises.followup: Support negative numbers by masking to 32 bits and converting the result back to a signed value.

exercises.title: All Subsets (bitmask)
exercises.prompt: Return every subset of `items` (each a list keeping the original order), using bitmasks instead of recursion. The order of the subsets does not matter.
hints: Count from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; each number is one subset.
Item i is in the subset when bit i of the mask is 1.
Approach: Enumerate masks 0 .. 2ⁿ − 1 and decode each.
mistakes: range(2 * n) instead of range(1 << n).
Testing mask & i instead of mask >> i & 1.
exercises.followup: Enumerate only the subsets of a given mask m: sub = m; while sub: ...; sub = (sub − 1) & m.

exercises.title: Two Single Numbers
exercises.prompt: Every value appears twice except two values that appear once. Return those two, smaller first, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hints: XOR of everything is a ^ b. Any 1 bit in it is a position where a and b differ.
Split the numbers by that bit: each group contains one of the two singles, and pairs stay together.
Approach: XOR all, isolate the lowest differing bit with x & −x, then XOR each half separately.
mistakes: Using a set: correct but O(n) space.
Isolating the bit with both & 1 (that bit may be 0).
exercises.followup: What if three numbers appear once?

exercises.title: Single Number II
exercises.prompt: Every value appears three times except one, which appears once. Return it with O(1) extra space. Values are 32-bit signed integers.
hints: Look at one bit position at a time. Count how many numbers have that bit set.
Triples contribute a multiple of 3; the remainder modulo 3 is the single number’s bit.
Approach: Count each of the 32 bits modulo 3, rebuild the number, and fix the sign.
mistakes: Forgetting the sign: bit 31 set means a negative number.
XOR, which only cancels pairs.
exercises.followup: Do it in one pass with two bitmasks ones and twos (a tiny state machine).

exercises.title: Zero is not a power of two
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bit-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
For n = 0, 0 & −1 is 0, so 0 is reported as a power of two: also require n > 0
Bit tricks often have one special case. Here it is 0 (and negative numbers): check n > 0 first.

exercises.title: Testing the wrong bit
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bit-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It ANDs with the number i instead of the mask 1 << i
Bit i has the value 2ⁱ, so the mask is `1 << i`. (In Python, & binds tighter than !=, so the brackets are not the problem here.)

exercises.title: The missing number goes missing
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test bit-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
The indexes only go up to n − 1, but the full range is 0..n: also XOR in n
The list holds n of the n + 1 numbers 0..n. XOR every number of the full range with every element; start result at n so n is included.

exercises.title: Range Sum Query (static)
exercises.prompt: Build a class `RangeSum(nums)` with a method `sum_range(l, r)` that returns `nums[l] + … + nums[r]` in O(1). The list never changes.
hints: Precompute running totals once in __init__.
sum(l..r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l].
Approach: Prefix sums with a leading 0.
exercises.cx: O(n) to build, O(1) per query
constraints: up to 10^4 calls to sum_range, 0 ≤ l ≤ r < n
mistakes: Summing the slice in every query (O(n) each).
Off-by-one: prefix[r] − prefix[l] misses nums[r].
exercises.followup: Do the same for a 2D matrix (rq-region-sum).

exercises.title: Apply Range Additions
exercises.prompt: Start with n zeros. Each update `(l, r, v)` adds v to every position from l to r inclusive. Return the final list, in O(n + number of updates).
hints: Looping over every range is O(n) per update. Record only where each change starts and stops.
diff[l] += v and diff[r + 1] −= v, then take running sums.
Approach: Difference array plus one prefix-sum pass.
mistakes: diff of length n: diff[r + 1] fails when r = n − 1.
Rebuilding with the extra last cell included.
exercises.followup: Range additions on a 2D grid: a 2D difference array with four corner updates.

exercises.title: Car Pooling
exercises.prompt: Each trip is `[passengers, start, end]`: they get in at km start and out at km end (so they are not in the car at km end). Can a car with `capacity` seats do all trips?
hints: Only the points where people get in or out matter.
Record +people at start and −people at end, then sweep and keep a running load.
Approach: Difference array over kilometres (a sweep line).
exercises.cx: O(n + K) time where K = 1001 kilometres
mistakes: Subtracting at end + 1: passengers leave AT km end.
Checking only the starting points of trips.
exercises.followup: If kilometres go up to 10⁹, sort the 2n events instead of using an array.

exercises.title: Flight Bookings
exercises.prompt: There are n flights numbered 1..n. Booking `[first, last, seats]` reserves that many seats on every flight from first to last. Return the total seats reserved on each flight.
hints: This is "apply range additions" with 1-based positions.
Allocate n + 2 cells so diff[last + 1] always exists.
Approach: Difference array with 1-based indexes.
mistakes: Mixing 0-based and 1-based flight numbers.
Returning the difference array instead of the running sums.
exercises.followup: Answer "how many seats on flight k?" online while bookings keep arriving (use a Fenwick tree with range-update, point-query).

exercises.title: 2D Region Sums
exercises.prompt: Given a matrix and a list of queries `(r1, c1, r2, c2)`, return the sum of each rectangle (inclusive corners). Precompute so that each query is O(1).
hints: Build P[r][c] = sum of everything above and to the left (inclusion–exclusion: add top and left, subtract the overlap).
A rectangle sum is one big prefix minus two strips plus the corner subtracted twice.
Approach: 2D prefix sums with an extra zero row and column.
exercises.cx: O(rows · cols) to build, O(1) per query
mistakes: Forgetting to add back P[r1][c1] (subtracted twice).
Off-by-one between matrix and P indexes.
exercises.followup: Support point updates too (2D Fenwick tree).

exercises.title: Build a Fenwick Tree
exercises.prompt: Implement `Fenwick(n)` for positions 0..n − 1 with `add(i, delta)`, `prefix_sum(i)` (sum of positions 0..i) and `range_sum(l, r)`, each in O(log n).
hints: Store a list of n + 1 zeros and shift positions by 1, because i & −i is 0 for i = 0.
add climbs with i += i & −i; prefix_sum descends with i −= i & −i; range_sum is a difference of two prefixes.
Approach: Binary indexed tree with 1-based internal indexes.
exercises.cx: O(log n) per operation, O(n) space
mistakes: Using 0-based indexes inside the loops (i & −i is 0: an infinite loop).
range_sum(l, r) computed as prefix_sum(r) − prefix_sum(l), which drops position l.
exercises.followup: Build the tree in O(n) from an initial list instead of n calls to add.

tests.label: 2,000 random updates and queries compared with a plain list

exercises.title: Range Sum Query (mutable)
exercises.prompt: Build `NumArray(nums)` with `update(i, value)` (set nums[i] to value) and `sum_range(l, r)`, both in O(log n). Use a Fenwick tree or a segment tree.
hints: update sets a value, but a Fenwick tree adds: add (value − old value).
Keep a copy of the current values to know the old value.
Approach: Fenwick tree storing differences, plus the current array.
exercises.cx: O(log n) per operation, O(n log n) to build this way
mistakes: Adding value instead of value − old (the update then accumulates).
Rebuilding prefix sums on every update: O(n).
exercises.followup: Implement the same class with an iterative segment tree and compare the code.

tests.label: [1, 3, 5]: sum, then update(1, 2) and sum again
updating to the same value twice
3,000 random updates and queries compared with a plain list

exercises.title: Segment Tree for Range Minimum
exercises.prompt: Build `MinTree(nums)` with `update(i, value)` and `query(l, r)` returning the minimum of nums[l..r] inclusive, both in O(log n).
hints: Store leaves at tree[n + i]; parent p holds min(tree[2p], tree[2p + 1]).
Query bottom-up with a half-open range [l, r): when l is a right child take it and move right; when r is odd, step left and take it.
Approach: Iterative segment tree of size 2n with bottom-up query.
exercises.cx: O(n) build, O(log n) per update and query, O(n) space
mistakes: Using a Fenwick tree with "prefix minus prefix": min has no inverse.
Forgetting to update ancestors after a point update.
Mixing inclusive and half-open ranges.
exercises.followup: Add range assignment ("set l..r to v") with lazy propagation.

tests.label: 3,000 random updates and queries on an odd-sized list, compared with min()

exercises.title: Count Smaller Numbers After Self
exercises.prompt: Return a list where element i is the number of elements to the right of nums[i] that are strictly smaller.
hints: Walk from right to left and keep track of the values seen so far.
A Fenwick tree over value ranks answers "how many seen values are smaller?" in O(log n). Compress values to ranks 1..m first.
Approach: Coordinate compression + Fenwick tree of counts, scanning from the right.
exercises.cx: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
mistakes: O(n²) double loop: too slow for 10⁵.
Counting equal values as smaller (query rank − 1, not rank).
Forgetting to reverse the result.
exercises.followup: Count inversions of the whole list (the sum of this output) with merge sort instead.

exercises.title: Off the end of the difference array
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test rq-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
When r is the last index, r + 1 is out of range: make diff one cell longer (and ignore the extra cell)
Allocate n + 1 cells so diff[r + 1] always exists, and rebuild only the first n.

exercises.title: Range sum misses the last element
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test rq-d3` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
prefix[k] is the sum of the first k values, so l..r inclusive is prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
Write down what prefix[k] means, then the indexes follow: elements l..r are the first r + 1 values minus the first l.

exercises.title: The update that went the wrong way
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test rq-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
add walks downwards like a query; it must climb with i += i & −i (while i ≤ n) to reach every node covering i
An update must touch every node whose range contains i: those are found by adding the lowest set bit.

exercises.title: Assign Cookies
exercises.prompt: Child i is content with a cookie of size ≥ `greed[i]`. Each child gets at most one cookie. Maximise content children.
hints: Sort both lists.
Give cookies in increasing size to the least greedy child still waiting.
Approach: Sort + greedy two pointers.

exercises.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
exercises.prompt: You may buy and sell many times (hold at most one share). Return the maximum profit.
hints: A long rise equals the sum of its daily rises.
Collect every positive day-to-day difference.
Approach: Greedy: take every upward step.

exercises.title: Merge Intervals
exercises.prompt:
Merge all overlapping intervals and return them sorted by start.

`[[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]` → `[[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]`
hints: Sort by start first.
Compare each interval with the LAST merged block only.
Approach: Sort, then extend or start a new block.

exercises.title: Insert Interval
exercises.prompt: `intervals` is sorted and non-overlapping. Insert `new`, merging where needed.
hints: Three phases: intervals before the new one, the ones that overlap it, the ones after.
Approach: Linear three-phase scan.

exercises.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
exercises.prompt: Return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap (touching at an end point is fine).
hints: Keeping the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for the others.
Sort by end time; keep an interval if it starts after the last kept one ends.
Approach: Greedy by earliest end (activity selection).

exercises.title: Interval List Intersections
exercises.prompt: Two lists of sorted, disjoint closed intervals. Return their intersections.
hints: Two pointers, one per list.
Overlap = [max of starts, min of ends] if non-empty; advance the interval that ends first.
Approach: Two pointers over both lists.

exercises.title: Jump Game
exercises.prompt: `nums[i]` is the maximum jump length from i. Can you reach the last index from index 0?
hints: You do not need to know WHICH jumps to take.
Track the farthest index reachable so far.
Approach: Greedy farthest reach.

exercises.title: Jump Game II
exercises.prompt: The last index is always reachable. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach it.
hints: Think in BFS levels: all indexes reachable with j jumps form a range.
When you reach the end of the current range, you must take another jump; the new range ends at the farthest reach seen.
Approach: Greedy BFS-by-ranges.

exercises.title: Gas Station
exercises.prompt: Stations in a circle: `gas[i]` fuel available, `cost[i]` to reach the next station. Return the start index to complete the circuit, or -1 (the answer is unique if it exists).
hints: If total gas < total cost, it is impossible.
If you run out at station i starting from s, no station between s and i works either: restart at i + 1.
Approach: One-pass greedy restart.

exercises.title: Partition Labels
exercises.prompt:
Split the string into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part. Return the part sizes.

`"ababcbacadefegdehijhklij"` → `[9, 7, 8]`
hints: Record the last index of every letter.
Extend the current part to the farthest last-index of its letters; cut when you reach it.
Approach: Greedy extension, like merging intervals.

exercises.title: Merging unsorted intervals
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test pt-d1` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
It never sorts, so overlaps between non-neighbouring intervals are missed
merge([[8, 10], [1, 9]]) returns two blocks instead of [[1, 10]].

exercises.title: Greedy by the wrong key
exercises.prompt: This code has a bug. The tests below describe what it should do. Run the tests, find the bug and fix it.
hints: Run `python dsa.py test pt-d2` and compare the first failing case with what you expected.
Sorting by start lets one long early meeting block many short ones; sort by END time instead
max_meetings([[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]]) returns 1, but 2 meetings fit.
